newsitem.title: CONGO: Rwanda, Uganda boycott regional talks - officials.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda, Uganda boycott regional talks - officials.

text.p: Rwanda and Uganda, accused by Zaire of aggression, boycotted a regional summit on Tuesday on resolving conflicts, conference officials said.
The one-day summit was hosted by Congo's President Pascal Lisouba within the framework of a United Nations committee dealing with security in the Great Lakes region of Central Africa.
"President Lisouba sent envoys to Uganda and Rwanda to persuade them to attend," a Congolese official told Reuters.
"I do not know what the followup was but they must be playing at empty-chair politics," the said.

Burundi's military strongman Pierre Buyoya, whose country is also regarded as an enemy by Zaire, shared the platform with Zairean Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo, who repeated charges against Zaire's neighbours.
Zaire says the Tutsi-dominated armies of Rwanda and Burundi are helping its ethnic Tutsis, who launched a rebellion in eastern Zaire in October and have seized a swathe of territory.
Uganda admitted at the weekend that its troops occupied positions in Zaire but said their objective was to hit Ugandan rebels based in Zaire and aided by the host state.
"The aim of these aggressors is to create a Hutuland on the eastern flank of Zaire," Kengo said.
Both Rwanda and Burundi still have large numbers of their Hutu people living as refugees in Zaire despite the mass return home of about half the one million Rwandans two weeks ago.
Zaire accuses the Tutsi leadership of the two states of not wanting rival Hutus back home. Rwanda and Burundi deny this.
Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania were invited as non-members of the committee but all three failed to turn up.

Delegates said the meeting appeared to have achieved little concrete in defusing the Zairean conflict, although it reiterated the committee's call for respect for the integrity of borders of member states.
The meeting also appealed for the lifting of regional sanctions imposed on Burundi at a summit in Arusha, Tanzania, following Buyoya's coup last July.

"Noting steps taken by the Burundian government towards re-establishing democracy, we urge parties to the Arusha accords to lift the embargo which largely affects the Burundian people," a summit communique said.
